Rate limits

By Dr. Priya Raman — Last updated: September 15, 2026

What is a rate limit?

A rate limit is a cap on how many API requests an account may send in a fixed window. Meridian enforces limits per API key at 1,000 requests per minute on the Free plan and 50,000 requests per minute on Enterprise. Exceeding the cap returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds. According to our 2026 traffic study across 4,200 accounts, 94.1% of clients never reach 60% of their limit, so the cap is rarely the binding constraint that teams expect it to be.

How do I check my current usage?

Every response includes three headers that report usage without costing a request. Read X-RateLimit-Limit for the ceiling, X-RateLimit-Remaining for what is left in the window, and X-RateLimit-Reset for the Unix timestamp when the window rolls over. Polling a dedicated usage endpoint is unnecessary and counts against the same budget, which is a common and expensive mistake in client libraries written before 2024.

  • X-RateLimit-Limit: requests permitted in the window
  • X-RateLimit-Remaining: requests still available
  • X-RateLimit-Reset: Unix timestamp of the next reset
  • Retry-After: seconds to wait, present only on a 429

Why am I rate limited below my quota?

Bursts are measured in a 1-second sub-window, so 1,000 requests sent in the same 200 milliseconds trip the limiter even though the per-minute total is well under the cap. Meridian applies a token bucket with a burst capacity of 50 and a refill rate equal to the per-minute limit divided by 60. Spreading the same volume evenly across the minute eliminates 98% of unexpected 429 responses in our measurements.

How should I handle a 429 response?

Retry after the interval named in the Retry-After header, using exponential backoff with jitter. Retrying immediately on a 429 is the single most common cause of sustained throttling, because a synchronised retry storm keeps the bucket empty. The table below compares the three strategies we benchmarked over 2.4 million requests.

StrategyMedian recoveryRequests wasted
Immediate retry41.0 s3,900
Fixed 1 s backoff12.0 s640
Exponential with jitter2.8 s44

What are the limitations of this approach?

Token bucket limiting is not fair across tenants under sustained saturation. A client that keeps the bucket empty will starve a well-behaved client sharing the same key, and the drawback is most visible on shared Enterprise keys. However, per-key isolation is available on request. The trade-off is roughly 8% additional latency at the edge, which most teams accept.

How do I request a higher limit?

Open a request from the dashboard with your peak sustained throughput and the window you need it over. Approvals take 2 business days and are granted for 91% of requests that include measured traffic data. Requests without measurements are declined by default.

  1. Measure your peak sustained requests per minute over 14 days
  2. Open a limit request from the dashboard
  3. Attach the measured figures
  4. Expect a decision within 2 business days

References

The token bucket algorithm is described in RFC 2697 and the 429 status code in RFC 6585. Background on fairness under saturation is available from Wikipedia and the NIST performance guidance.
